title: The grave

segments.voice: Yesterday: mawt, death, and the soul at peace called back to its Lord.

Two seas, loosed by their Lord, run up against each other and meet. Water against water. The Qur'an, in Surah ar-Rahman, says of them, in Pickthall's words: "There is a barrier between them. They encroach not." The Arabic for that barrier is barzakh. Hold on to it, because the same word turns up somewhere much quieter. Not at the shoreline. At the graveside.
screen: `TWO SEAS, SIDE BY SIDE.` → `A BARRIER BETWEEN THEM.` → `THE SAME WORD, AT THE GRAVE.`

segments.voice: In Surah al-Mu'minun, someone at the point of death begs to be sent back, to do the good they left undone. The answer is no, and then a phrase, Pickthall again: "and behind them is a barrier until the day when they are raised." Barzakh. So the word that holds two seas apart also names the stretch between dying and rising: not this world any more, not yet the Day. The in-between. It's also spoken of as the grave, al-qabr, though the barzakh is more than a hole in the ground. What happens there? The Qur'an says little in detail, and the hadith say more. One in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Ibn 'Umar, says that when a person dies, their place in the next life is shown to them morning and evening, and they are told: this is your place, until Allah raises you. So the in-between is not empty waiting. It is waiting with a view. Since it's part of the unseen, al-ghayb, scholars are careful to say the hadith describe it without explaining how. And notice what this does to a graveyard. A hadith in Sahih Muslim has the Prophet, peace be upon him, going out at night to the graveyard of al-Baqi' in Medina, greeting the dead with peace and asking forgiveness for them. He greets them because, in this teaching, the people in those graves are not gone. They are across a barrier: like the two seas, close, side by side, and kept apart.
screen: `SEND ME BACK. THE ANSWER IS NO.` · `A BARRIER UNTIL THE DAY OF RAISING.` · `WAITING, WITH A VIEW.` · then, large: `GREETING THE ONES ACROSS THE BARRIER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who has died, someone you knew or someone whose name you only heard, and think of them not as gone but as across a barrier. If you pray, greet them as the Prophet greeted the dead at al-Baqi', with peace, and ask forgiveness for them; if not, say their name once and wish them well. And if missing someone is too heavy to carry alone, in the US call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.
Barzakh. A barrier; in Muslim teaching, the in-between of the grave, from death until the Day of rising. Today's word.
Your line: the in-between. Close, side by side, and kept apart, like the two seas. That's day twelve fifty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims visit graves to remember the hereafter, greet the dead with salam, and ask forgiveness for them; the time between death and the Day of Resurrection is called the barzakh, or the life of the grave.

chat.says: What happens to people between dying and the Day of Judgment?
options: They're in the barzakh, an in-between, shown their place morning and evening.
They're sent back to do the good they left undone, then return.
They wait in an empty dark, with no sense of what's to come.
chat.meaning: Barzakh names the stretch between dying and rising. A hadith in Bukhari says the dead are shown their place morning and evening: waiting with a view.
